source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, Meditation XVII

source.excerpt: No man is an Iland, intire of it selfe; every man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine… any mans death diminishes me, because I am involved in Mankinde; And therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; It tolls for thee.
trail: The exact wording sits in Meditation XVII, which closes with “any man’s death diminishes me… it tolls for thee.”
Devotions upon Emergent Occasions was written in December 1623 during Donne’s recovery from illness and first published in 1624.
The 1624 original reads “No man is an Iland… I am involved in Mankinde” — the popular quote just modernises the spelling.
source.excerptNote: Donne’s original 1624 spelling. Modern editions regularise it to “No man is an island… any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind; and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.”
source.rightsNote: First published in 1624, Devotions upon Emergent Occasions is long in the public domain worldwide. The modern-spelling wording adds no new copyrightable authorship — it merely regularises Donne’s own 17th-century text.

author.bio: John Donne (1572–1631) was the leading English metaphysical poet and, from 1621, Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral. He wrote his Devotions upon Emergent Occasions in December 1623 while recovering from a life-threatening fever, meditating on mortality and human interconnection. Meditation XVII — source of both “no man is an island” and “for whom the bell tolls” — is his most quoted prose.

items.why: The lines are prose from Meditation XVII, a devotional essay. The familiar line-broken “No Man Is an Island” poem is a modern rearrangement of Donne’s continuous prose.
Hemingway’s 1940 novel took its title and epigraph from this passage; the words are Donne’s, written more than three centuries earlier.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine John Donne — prose from Meditation XVII of the Devotions (1624), only modernised in spelling.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Donne wrote the Devotions in December 1623 as he lay gravely ill, listening to the church bells that tolled for the dying and dead of his parish. Meditation XVII turns that sound into an argument about human solidarity: because every person is “a part of the main,” another’s death is a loss to oneself.
The passage gave English two of its most enduring phrases — “no man is an island” and “for whom the bell tolls” — the latter immortalised again by Ernest Hemingway’s 1940 novel.
